store.0: I am a Computer Science major in my fourth year, taking higher-level courses such as advanced system design and quantum computing basics.
store.1: I am excited to share my experience in the Advanced Algorithms class. It is my favorite class this semester, and I am fascinated by the theoretical aspects of problem-solving. We have been exploring various approaches such as dynamic programming and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. The professor is excellent at explaining complex concepts in an intuitive manner, making the material more accessible. She presents a problem on the board, which initially seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then reveals a strategy to approximate a solution. Each class leaves me with a sense of intellectual stimulation and a desire to learn more.
store.2: I am currently taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is one of the most challenging classes this semester. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an exciting adventure as we collaborate with team members who have different coding styles and ideas. It's a great learning experience as we handle real-world issues such as concurrency, integration, and node failures. Although it can be nerve-wracking at times, like when we encountered a bug due to a misplaced bracket in the config file, the sense of accomplishment when we finally fixed it was immense.
store.3: I am taking an elective in Game Design, which is a must-take for me as a gamer at heart. The professor is from the industry and has worked on several indie games. We are learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, physics implementation, and user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and I enjoyed designing a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept. The challenge was to balance the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. It was rewarding to see the design come together successfully.
store.4: I initially found the Introduction to Quantum Computing class intimidating, but the professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Although there is a significant amount of linear algebra involved, it is balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're exploring algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. This class has been mind-blowing and has changed my approach to problem-solving.
store.5: The Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts based on sentiment analysis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface, and ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and staying organized. It's a lot, but if we can successfully complete it, I'll be incredibly proud.
store.6: I am taking a Philosophy of Mind elective, which is my last required non-CS course. This class explores the intersection of philosophy and AI, discussing topics like consciousness, the concept of mind, and its application to artificial intelligence. The class size is smaller, allowing for in-depth discussions and a change of pace from the coding-intensive nature of my other classes. It's refreshing to analyze abstract ideas and consider the ethical implications of creating AI systems that may simulate human thinking. In a recent assignment, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, such as subjective experiences like color or pain. This topic is significant in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe combining technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this course provides valuable insights.
store.7: My typical college schedule is quite packed. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before attending the Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are slightly lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be challenging if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually spend them working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also have undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's a demanding schedule, but I'm determined to make the most of my senior year.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone requires around 10 hours a week, and if we encounter bugs or issues with the model, it can take even longer. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another time-consuming task. My group meets at least twice a week to work on these projects, and we also rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating the schedules of five people can be a nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in purely academic projects without the pressures of a job environment. It's a great opportunity to learn and grow.
store.9: I'm having a great time this semester. Initially, I was intimidated by the tougher CS classes, but now I've developed better problem-solving and time management skills. Although I still have the occasional late night, especially when working on a deadline, it's no longer as daunting as it once was. As a senior, I've gained confidence in my abilities and know that with hard work and focus, I can overcome challenges. The classes are tough, but they're also incredibly rewarding. I feel like everything I'm doing now is directly contributing to my future career, and that's a wonderful feeling. I've learned to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. It's been an incredible journey so far.

It has given me insights into how knowledge is created in the tech world. I initially didn't consider research as an option, but a professor encouraged me to apply for a research assistant position in a data visualization lab. store.12: I am currently working in an interdisciplinary lab where computer scientists collaborate with experts from various fields such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. We aim to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. My main task involves creating front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This requires expertise in advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data. It's a challenging yet rewarding experience.
store.13: I worked on a research project that involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. The project involved aggregating and presenting daily temperature readings from buoys in the Pacific Ocean. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designed interfaces that allowed researchers to zoom into specific regions or timeframes. The project resulted in my co-authorship of a paper, which was a surreal and proud moment for me.
store.14: I have been working on immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. By providing an intuitive 3D representation of data, scientists can interact with it in a more immersive way, such as walking around, touching, and highlighting subsets. This approach is cutting-edge and requires experimentation with VR headsets, integration with engines like Unity or Unreal, and efficient data streaming into the 3D environment. It's a challenging yet exciting field, as there isn't a well-established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet. Every day, I'm forging my own path and learning as I go.
store.15: Research life is not just about coding away in a quiet corner. It involves a lot of reading and analyzing academic papers to find relevant information for solving specific problems. For example, when working on rendering volumetric data in VR, I need to search for similar attempts in conference proceedings or workshops. It can be overwhelming, but over time, I've learned to skim through papers effectively by reading the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine their relevance. Occasionally, when I find interesting techniques, I share them with the lab and we discuss how to incorporate them into our workflow. It's a collaborative process that helps us improve our research.
store.16: I have been working with a PhD student who is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He wants to integrate it with our VR platform to improve real-time performance. By using compression, we can reduce the need to load every single point of a huge climate dataset at once in VR. This is a practical approach that can enhance user experience. I find it fascinating to see how advanced theoretical concepts are applied in real-time scenarios. Our best brainstorming sessions often happen spontaneously, like during coffee breaks in the lab, where we discuss ways to offload processing to the GPU. It's inspiring to work alongside graduate students who are deeply immersed in their niche fields.
store.17: I have been involved in poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. I had to boil down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous about presenting, especially with the possibility of random professors or industry folks asking tough questions. However, it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People were genuinely interested in what I was doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they shared interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries, such as marketing analytics or architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.18: I have been involved in co-authoring two workshop papers and am currently working on a larger conference submission for the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS). The conference paper focuses on a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than with 2D charts. We conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recorded their times, and asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire. Now we're analyzing the data to determine if there's a statistically significant difference. The paper is a collaborative effort, with me handling the system architecture and prototype design, another team member writing about the user study methodology, and our PI weaving it all together. It's a balancing act, especially with my senior coursework and capstone project to manage.
store.19: I am currently considering working in the industry for a couple of years before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. I am drawn to the idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts are applied in real product development. My mentor in the lab suggested that stepping into industry can provide a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, which would be beneficial if I decide to return for a PhD with a more practical approach.
store.20: I have been involved in research for a while now, and it has been a rollercoaster ride. There have been times when I spent weeks on an approach that didn't pan out, or when I discovered that my idea had already been done and improved upon by a group in Europe. It can be frustrating, but the key is to adapt. I read existing papers, incorporate their findings, and look for new angles or applications. Research is all about building on the foundation laid by others. The sense of collaboration within our lab and among the global research community is truly special. It's a privilege to be part of this community and contribute to the advancement of knowledge.
store.21: A few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed, and we lost some vital data that wasn't fully backed up. It was a stressful experience, but it taught us the importance of having a reliable backup system. After that incident, we set up a better backup system and implemented checks to ensure we don't rely on a single point of failure. It was a bonding experience for the whole lab, and we learned a valuable lesson.

store.29: The campus culture is generally collaborative, with a strong sense of community and mutual support. While there are certainly competitive elements, especially among seniors, the overall atmosphere is one of cooperation and teamwork. The campus hackathon is a prime example of this spirit. Thousands of students from diverse backgrounds come together for 24 or 36 hours, united by their passion for coding and innovation. It's a time for learning, collaboration, and celebration, where beginners can learn from experienced peers and advanced teams push the boundaries of technology. The bonds formed during these events are truly special, as seen in the friendships forged during the hackathon. It's this shared experience and camaraderie that make campus life so vibrant and memorable.
store.30: Dorm life can be a significant part of campus culture, especially for students who live in dorms specifically designed for engineering majors like "The Engi-House". The common lounge becomes a hub for late-night coding sessions, e-sports tournaments, and other activities. It's a great place to find study buddies or get help from peers who have already tackled similar assignments. Additionally, dorm life offers opportunities for socializing, such as potlucks, movie nights, and talent shows. These experiences help create a sense of community and camaraderie among residents.
store.31: I volunteer at outreach events, such as the "Tech for Good" day where local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. I help run mini-workshops on topics like web development or basic Python. It's fulfilling to see younger students get excited when they create a simple game or animated webpage. These events not only provide a positive experience for the students but also showcase the campus's commitment to engaging with the community and inspiring the next generation in STEM fields.
store.32: The social scene on campus is lively and diverse. While some students participate in Greek life, others find their social circles through specialized clubs based on their interests. For example, a friend who is passionate about robotics joined the Robotics Team and found a close-knit group of like-minded individuals. Similarly, I have formed strong bonds with members of the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. These clubs provide a platform for socializing beyond academics, allowing us to share laughter, discuss non-academic topics, and plan weekend activities together. It's a great way to balance academic rigor with social connections and personal growth.
store.33: Senior Week is a significant tradition on campus, marking the final stretch before graduation. It includes events like a formal dance, a carnival, and a photo shoot where seniors wear their caps and gowns around iconic landmarks. It's a bittersweet experience, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a sense of sadness that the journey is coming to an end. Many seniors have shared that it's one of the best weeks of their college life, creating lasting memories before they scatter. I'm excited and a bit anxious for this experience, knowing that it will be a memorable conclusion to my time as a student.
store.34: The Rivalry Game is a significant campus tradition where our sports teams face off against our biggest rival college in various sports. It brings a lot of energy and excitement to the campus. People show their school spirit by wearing school colors, painting their faces, and waving banners. The night before the big football game, we have a massive pep rally with fireworks, making it a spectacular event. Even if you're not a sports fan, the campus vibe is electric during this time. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer together. Whether we win or lose, the campus comes together to celebrate or commiserate. It's a unifying moment for everyone, regardless of their majors or interests.
store.35: The recognition of our school's e-sports team has been a significant development. It's great to see a broader definition of campus sports, with the e-sports arena hosting tournaments and attracting a large audience. The energy and community surrounding these events are truly vibrant, showcasing the evolving nature of campus life. It's exciting to be part of this shift and witness the growth of e-sports as a legitimate part of the campus experience.
store.36: The Midnight Breakfast event during finals week is a heartwarming tradition that brings the campus together. It's a time for stressed-out students to take a break from studying and enjoy some pancakes and cereal with their peers. Professors and the school band often join in, adding to the festive atmosphere. This event serves as a reminder that even during high-pressure times, we're not alone and that the campus community is there to support us. It's a testament to the genuine effort to create a positive and inclusive environment for all students.
store.37: Campus life is what you make of it. By exploring, approaching new people, and joining clubs, you can greatly enrich your experience. It's easy to get caught up in academics, especially in a demanding major like Computer Science. However, taking the time to attend events, volunteer, and connect with various communities has been incredibly rewarding. I've had memorable moments like late-night coding, silly game nights in the dorm, Tech Fest presentations, hackathon adrenaline, and cheering at the Rivalry Game. It's been a whirlwind, but I wouldn't trade it for anything. If you ever want a tour or want to meet some club members, feel free to ask. There's truly something for everyone here, and I'm glad I finally opened up to all the campus has to offer.

I want to apply my knowledge in a commercial setting for a while before committing to a PhD. Some peers suggest doing a part-time master's while working, while others recommend going all-in if I decide to pursue a graduate degree. It's a complex decision.

It's not just about coding; it's about collaborating with others, brainstorming solutions, prototyping, and iterating until they work. I want to work in an environment that encourages cross-functional collaboration with designers, data scientists, product managers, and domain experts from non-tech fields. A full-time engineering position typically offers a decent salary, which would help me achieve this goal. In contrast, pursuing a graduate degree can be more financially uncertain, with varying funding options and potential tuition costs. I am considering the practical benefits of industry employment, including financial stability and career momentum, while also weighing the potential benefits of further education. It's a complex decision.

The advanced courses I'm taking, such as Advanced Algorithms and Distributed Systems, are helping me build confidence for the technical interviews.
